title: JESUS SAID, “I WILL BUILD MY CHURCH.” SO WHY ARE THERE SO MANY? THE QUESTION CHRISTIANS CAN NO LONGER AFFORD TO IGNORE.
paragraphs: JESUS SAID, “I WILL BUILD MY CHURCH.” SO WHY ARE THERE SO MANY? THE QUESTION CHRISTIANS CAN NO LONGER AFFORD TO IGNORE.

One Savior. One Cross. One Body. Thousands of Denominational Labels. Did Jesus Establish One Visible Church, or Can Different Denominations Truly Belong to Him? The Answer May Challenge Your Loyalty, Expose Our Divisions, and Change How You See the Family of God Forever.
Imagine standing before Jesus Christ.

Not before your pastor. Not before your bishop. Not before your denomination's founders. Not before a church council, a theological professor, or the people who taught you everything you believe about Christianity.
Just you.
And Jesus.
The One whose hands still bear the scars of the price He paid to redeem sinners.
Now imagine Him asking you a question.
“Did you love My Church as I commanded you to love her? Or did you spend your life defending your group while forgetting the people I died to save?”
That is not a quotation from Scripture. But it is a question worth allowing Scripture to examine.
Because somewhere between the empty tomb and the thousands of church signs scattered across our cities, something happened that should make every follower of Jesus stop and think.
We became very good at explaining why we are different.
But have we become equally good at demonstrating why we belong to the same Lord?
A Catholic walks into a Protestant church and wonders whether the worship is legitimate.
A Protestant enters a Catholic church and wonders whether the Gospel is being obscured.
An Orthodox Christian looks at both and asks what happened to the ancient faith.

A Baptist questions infant baptism. A Pentecostal questions why some Christians seem uncomfortable with spiritual gifts. A Reformed believer challenges teachings about salvation. A non-denominational Christian says, “I just follow Jesus,” while often inheriting theological traditions without realizing it.
And somewhere in the middle of all these arguments sits a person who has never truly known Christ.
Watching.
Listening.
Wondering.
“If Jesus is the Prince of Peace, why does His family seem so divided?”
That question should trouble us.
Not because every disagreement is sinful.
Not because truth does not matter.
But because Jesus Himself prayed for the unity of those who would believe in Him.
And His prayer was not casual.
It was spoken on the night before His crucifixion.
“That they all may be one; as thou, Father, art in me, and I in thee, that they also may be one in us: that the world may believe that thou hast sent me.” — John 17:21, KJV
Read those final words again.
That the world may believe.
Jesus connected the visible love and unity of His followers to the world's recognition of His divine mission.
And that means our divisions are not merely an internal family problem.
They affect our witness.

But before we rush to condemn denominations, before we declare that only one institution can possibly be the true Church, or that all denominations are equally faithful simply because they use the name of Jesus, we need to return to a place where our arguments must become quiet.
The Word of God.
Because the Church does not belong to the loudest defender of tradition.
The Church belongs to Jesus Christ.
And He has already told us something extraordinary about it.
In Matthew 16, Jesus asks His disciples who they believe He is.
Peter answers:
“Thou art the Christ, the Son of the living God.” — Matthew 16:16, KJV
Jesus then declares:
“And I say also unto thee, That thou art Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church; and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it.” — Matthew 16:18, KJV
There is something powerful here that is easy to overlook.
Jesus did not say, “You will build your church.”
He did not say, “The strongest religious institution will build My church.”
He said:
“I will build my church.”
The Builder is Christ.
The ownership is Christ's.
The promise is Christ's.
And the victory belongs to Christ.
But the original Greek text reveals something important about the question we are asking.
Jesus says:
κἀγὼ δέ σοι λέγω ὅτι σὺ εἶ Πέτρος, καὶ ἐπὶ ταύτῃ τῇ πέτρᾳ οἰκοδομήσω μου τὴν ἐκκλησίαν.
Kagō de soi legō hoti sy ei Petros, kai epi tautē tē petra oikodomēsō mou tēn ekklēsian.
“And I also say to you that you are Peter, and upon this rock I will build My church.”
The word ἐκκλησίαν (ekklēsian) is the accusative form of ekklēsia, commonly translated “church” or “assembly.”
In this context, Jesus is speaking of the community that belongs to Him.
Not merely a building.
Not merely a religious brand.
Not merely a collection of individuals who privately believe in God.
A people called together under His authority.
The singular matters.
Jesus says μου τὴν ἐκκλησίαν — mou tēn ekklēsian — “My church.”
But we must be careful.
The singular word “church” establishes the unity of Christ's people. By itself, it does not settle every historical dispute about how that unity must be institutionally expressed.
And this is where the conversation becomes uncomfortable.
Because sincere Christians have disagreed for centuries about the meaning of the rock upon which Jesus promised to build His Church.
Catholic theology understands Peter's role and the authority entrusted to him as foundational to the continuing visible structure of the Church, including the papacy.
Eastern Orthodox theology affirms the apostolic foundations and visible continuity of the Church while rejecting the Catholic understanding of universal papal jurisdiction.

Protestant interpreters have commonly emphasized Peter's confession of Christ, Christ Himself as the ultimate foundation, or Peter's foundational role without accepting the later Catholic claims concerning the papacy.
And these are not trivial differences.

The Greek distinction between Πέτρος (Petros) and πέτρα (petra) has often been discussed in these debates. Yet it would be misleading to claim that the difference alone conclusively proves one interpretation. Jesus may have originally spoken these words in Aramaic, where kepha could serve for both Peter's name and “rock.” The precise original Aramaic wording of this exchange has not been preserved independently.
Whatever interpretation one holds, no faithful reading should remove Jesus from the center of the passage.
Peter is not the Savior.
The Church is not the Savior.
No succession of human leaders can replace the crucified and risen Lord.
Jesus Christ is the One who builds and preserves His Church.
And when we turn to the apostle Paul, the mystery becomes even more profound.

“There is one body, and one Spirit, even as ye are called in one hope of your calling; One Lord, one faith, one baptism, One God and Father of all, who is above all, and through all, and in you all.” — Ephesians 4:4–6, KJV
In the Greek, Paul begins with a declaration:
ἓν σῶμα καὶ ἓν πνεῦμα.
Hen sōma kai hen pneuma.
“One body and one Spirit.”
Not many competing bodies belonging to different saviors.
One body.
And the word ἕν (hen) means “one.”
Paul continues with a rhythm that leaves no room for divided ultimate allegiance.
One Lord.
One faith.
One baptism.
One God and Father.
Notice what Paul does not say.
He does not say that every disagreement between Christians is meaningless.
He does not say that doctrine can be sacrificed for the appearance of peace.
He does not say that every religious organization claiming Christ necessarily teaches His Gospel faithfully.
But neither does he give Christians permission to turn their secondary identities into rival kingdoms.
The unity of the Church is rooted in the unity of the God we worship.
And this brings us to a question that is more personal than denominational statistics.
What if some of us have become more loyal to the name on our church sign than to the Lord whose name we confess?
That question is not an accusation against every denominational Christian.
Many believers deeply love Jesus and faithfully serve Him within their traditions.
But all of us need to examine our hearts.
Because denominational pride can become a form of spiritual blindness.
And spiritual blindness is particularly dangerous when it disguises itself as faithfulness.
Think about the church in Corinth.
The believers were already forming factions around respected leaders.
Some claimed Paul.
Others claimed Apollos.
Others claimed Cephas.
Paul confronted them with a question that still pierces the Church today.
“Is Christ divided? was Paul crucified for you? or were ye baptized in the name of Paul?” — 1 Corinthians 1:13, KJV
Imagine replacing those names with our modern identities.
Was your denomination crucified for you?
Did your favorite preacher carry your sins to Calvary?
Did your theological tradition rise from the dead on the third day?
Did your church founder conquer death?
No.
Jesus did.
And if that truth does not humble us, we have not yet allowed the Cross to confront our pride.
But here is where we must resist an easy answer.
Some people respond to Christian division by saying, “Denominations do not matter. All that matters is Jesus.”
It sounds beautiful.
And it contains an important truth: no denominational label can save a soul.
But it can also conceal a serious problem.
The Jesus we claim to follow has revealed truths that matter.
The identity of Christ matters.
His bodily resurrection matters.
His saving work matters.
The authority of Scripture matters.
The meaning of the Gospel matters.
Baptism, the Lord's Supper, church leadership, worship, and the nature of the Church itself matter enough to deserve serious biblical examination.
Love does not require us to pretend that contradictions are agreements.
And unity is not strengthened by hiding theological differences beneath emotional language.
Paul urged believers to speak “the truth in love” (Ephesians 4:15).
Both words are necessary.
Truth without love can become a weapon.
Love without truth can become an excuse to avoid obedience.
But truth spoken in love builds up the body of Christ.
So can different denominations faithfully represent His body?
The answer requires an important distinction.
Christ has one body. Christians disagree about the visible boundaries and proper structure of that body.
Catholic teaching identifies the Church of Christ as subsisting in the Catholic Church, while recognizing elements of sanctification and truth outside its visible structure.
Eastern Orthodox Christians understand the fullness of the apostolic Church to be preserved in the Orthodox communion, with its sacramental and episcopal continuity.
Many Protestants understand the one universal Church as encompassing all who truly belong to Christ through faith, while local congregations and denominations may express that unity imperfectly.
These positions cannot simply be declared identical.
They make different claims about authority, sacraments, apostolic succession, and the Church's visible identity.
And it would be dishonest to suggest that Matthew 16:18 and Ephesians 4:4–6 alone resolve every one of those disputes.
But they do establish something no Christian should evade.
Jesus intended His people to belong to one body under one Lord.
And the New Testament gives that unity visible expression.
The first believers devoted themselves to apostolic teaching, fellowship, breaking bread, and prayers (Acts 2:42).
They shared life.
They cared for the needy.
They gathered for worship.
They submitted to spiritual oversight.
They were not simply isolated believers connected by a private spiritual feeling.
They were a recognizable community.
At the same time, the New Testament describes churches in Jerusalem, Antioch, Corinth, Ephesus, Philippi, and other places.
There were many local congregations.
But not many Christs.
There were different communities.
But not different Gospels that could all be equally true.
And when serious doctrinal disputes arose, the apostles did not simply shrug and say, “Everyone has their own interpretation.”
Acts 15 records a gathering in Jerusalem to address a controversy that threatened the unity and faithfulness of the early Church.
They examined the matter together.
They listened.
They appealed to God's work and the Scriptures.
They sought a faithful judgment.
That should tell us something.
Biblical unity is not the absence of conviction.
It is the pursuit of faithfulness to Christ together.
And now comes the part that may hurt.
Because it is easier to debate which Church has the strongest historical claim than to ask whether our own lives resemble the Church Jesus calls us to be.
We can defend apostolic succession while refusing to forgive someone who wounded us.
We can quote sola Scriptura while neglecting the Scriptures we claim to honor.
We can celebrate spiritual gifts while lacking the fruit of the Spirit.
We can insist that our worship is biblical while treating fellow believers with contempt.
We can explain justification, sanctification, and ecclesiology with impressive precision while our families are starving for patience, kindness, humility, and love.
We can be correct about a doctrine and still sin in the way we defend it.
And we can be sincere about our faith while still needing correction.
That is why the question of the true Church must never become an excuse to avoid the deeper question.
Am I truly following the Head of the Church?
Paul writes:
The Head is Jesus.
Not our preferred institution considered apart from Him.
Not our favorite theological personality.
Not our spiritual reputation.
Jesus.
The One who touched lepers when others withdrew.
The One who welcomed repentant sinners when respectable people were offended.
The One who confronted religious hypocrisy without surrendering truth.
The One who wept over Jerusalem.
The One who washed His disciples' feet.
The One who went willingly to the Cross.
And perhaps the most heartbreaking irony in all our divisions is this:
We sometimes fight over who represents the crucified Christ while refusing to demonstrate the humility of the crucified Christ.
We defend the Church He purchased with His blood while speaking about other people He loves as though they are beneath our compassion.
And somewhere, a wounded believer walks away from a congregation.
Not because Jesus failed.
But because the people claiming His name failed to reflect His character.
Perhaps that person is you.
Perhaps you were raised in a tradition where questions were treated as rebellion.
Perhaps you entered a different church and were made to feel that your entire spiritual history was worthless.
Perhaps you watched leaders protect reputations instead of wounded people.
Perhaps you were taught to fear every Christian outside your denomination.
Or perhaps you have become so exhausted by arguments about religion that you have quietly wondered whether following Jesus is even possible without becoming trapped in another conflict.
If that is you, hear this carefully.
The sins of Christians do not make the holiness of Christ disappear.
The failures of churches do not invalidate the resurrection.
And the existence of division does not mean Jesus has abandoned His people.
But neither should those truths be used to excuse abuse, silence legitimate questions, or demand loyalty to leaders who refuse accountability.
Jesus does not ask us to confuse institutional self-protection with faithfulness.
He calls His people to truth, repentance, justice, holiness, and love.
And sometimes that means confronting sin inside our own community before criticizing anyone else's.
Remember what Jesus said:
“By this shall all men know that ye are my disciples, if ye have love one to another.” — John 13:35, KJV
He did not say the world would recognize His disciples by the complexity of their arguments alone.
Or by the age of their institutions alone.
Or by the emotional intensity of their worship alone.
Or by the number of people attending their services.
He pointed to love.
Not sentimental love that ignores sin.
Not counterfeit love that abandons truth.
But the kind of love that bears burdens, seeks reconciliation, practices forgiveness, serves the vulnerable, and remains faithful to Christ.
And we need to be clear about something else.
Not every division is equally blameworthy, and not every separation can be healed by pretending that truth is negotiable.
Some Christians have separated over serious doctrinal convictions.
Others have separated because of corruption, coercion, abuse, or failures of leadership.
Some divisions involve questions of authority that centuries of theological dialogue have not resolved.
Some reflect human pride that should have been crucified long ago.
It would be simplistic to declare that every denomination exists because someone rebelled against God.
It would be equally simplistic to insist that the existence of thousands of Christian groups is exactly what Jesus intended.
Scripture calls us toward unity, not complacency about division.
And yet the unity we seek must be unity in Christ and His truth.
This is why the words of Ephesians 4 become even more demanding when we read what comes before the famous declaration of one body.
“With all lowliness and meekness, with longsuffering, forbearing one another in love; Endeavouring to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.” — Ephesians 4:2–3, KJV
Do you see it?
Before Paul speaks of one body, he speaks of humility.
Gentleness.
Patience.
Bearing with one another in love.
Why?
Because Christian unity is not merely a theological proposition to defend.
It is a spiritual responsibility to practice.
And nobody practices humility by constantly announcing their superiority.
Nobody practices patience by refusing to listen.
Nobody practices love by delighting in another believer's humiliation.
We must be willing to ask hard questions about doctrine.
But we must also be willing to ask hard questions about ourselves.
Have I mistaken inherited tradition for personal conviction?
Have I ever studied the strongest biblical arguments of Christians who disagree with me?
Have I used the word “heretic” carelessly?
Have I confused disagreement with hatred?
Have I treated another believer as an enemy simply because we differ on church government, baptism, or worship?
Have I allowed my desire to win arguments to become greater than my desire to honor Jesus?
And perhaps the most uncomfortable question:
If Jesus examined the way I defend His Church, would He recognize His own character in me?
That question does not belong only to Catholics.
Or Orthodox Christians.
Or Protestants.
Or non-denominational believers.
It belongs to all of us.
Because all of us need grace.
And grace does not mean that truth becomes unimportant.
Grace means that sinners who cannot save themselves are invited to come to the Savior who can.
This is where our theme becomes more than a phrase.
The scandal is not merely that Christians disagree.
The scandal is that people redeemed by undeserved mercy can sometimes become merciless toward one another.
The scandal is that we can preach reconciliation with God while resisting reconciliation with our brothers and sisters.
The scandal is that we can celebrate the Cross while protecting the pride that the Cross exposes.
But grace speaks another word.
Grace says that repentance is still possible.
Grace says that hardened hearts can soften.
Grace says that truth can be defended without cruelty.
Grace says that a wounded believer can find healing without pretending the wound never happened.
Grace says that people divided by history can still speak honestly, listen carefully, and pursue peace without denying their convictions.
And above all, grace declares that Jesus Christ remains faithful even when His followers fail.
He is not waiting helplessly for human institutions to rescue His mission.
He is the risen Lord.
The Shepherd who knows His sheep.
The Savior who gave Himself for His people.
Paul writes:
There is the measure of His commitment.
Not a slogan.
Not a denominational manifesto.
His blood.
And if Christ loved the Church enough to give Himself for her, how can we claim to love Him while treating His people carelessly?
This does not require us to surrender discernment.
Jesus warned about false prophets.
The apostles warned about false teaching.
The New Testament repeatedly calls believers to guard the Gospel.
But the same Scriptures command us to pursue peace, correct with gentleness, and love one another sincerely.
The faithful Christian must hold these commands together.
Never sacrificing truth to purchase a superficial peace.
Never sacrificing love to satisfy religious pride.
So what should you do if you are wondering whether your own denomination faithfully represents the body of Christ?
Do not begin with fear.
Begin with Jesus.
Read the Gospels carefully.
Study the apostolic teaching.
Examine what your church teaches about Christ, salvation, the Scriptures, worship, holiness, and the nature of the Church.
Learn the history of your tradition.
Listen fairly to serious Christians who disagree.
Ask whether the claims of your community can withstand honest biblical and historical examination.
Seek leaders who welcome sincere questions and demonstrate integrity.
Look for a congregation where Christ is faithfully proclaimed, Scripture is taken seriously, worship is reverent, discipleship is practiced, and love is more than a word painted on the wall.
And remember that visible beauty, ancient continuity, passionate worship, intellectual sophistication, or impressive growth, considered alone, cannot settle every question of faithfulness.
Do not choose a church merely because it makes you comfortable.
But do not remain in a spiritually harmful environment merely because someone tells you that leaving would mean abandoning God.
Seek truth.
Seek wisdom.
Seek the Lord.
And do so with the humility of someone who knows that only Christ is infallible.
Perhaps you are reading this as a Catholic.
You do not need to abandon your convictions to recognize that contempt for other Christians is contrary to Christ's command to love.
Perhaps you are Orthodox.
You can take the historical and sacramental claims of your Church seriously while remembering that humility is not optional.
Perhaps you are Protestant.
You can remain deeply committed to the authority of Scripture and the Gospel of grace while refusing to treat every Christian outside your tradition as an enemy.
Perhaps you belong to a non-denominational congregation.
You can love the simplicity of identifying as a follower of Jesus while recognizing that your church still has interpretations, practices, and theological commitments that deserve examination.
And perhaps you do not belong to any church at all.
Perhaps you have been watching Christianity from a distance because you cannot understand why people who claim to follow one Savior disagree so fiercely.
Please do not judge Jesus solely by the worst behavior of those who claim His name.
Read His words.
Examine His life.
Consider His death and resurrection.
Listen to His invitation.
Because the center of Christianity is not the claim that Christians have always behaved faithfully.
The center is the good news that Jesus Christ came to save sinners.
“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast.” — Ephesians 2:8–9, KJV
Salvation is not purchased through denominational membership.
It is not earned by winning theological debates.
It is not secured by financial contributions.
It is God's gift, received through faith in Jesus Christ.
And the grace that saves us also calls us into a transformed life.
A life of repentance.
A life of obedience.
A life of love.
A life in which our loyalty to Jesus becomes greater than our desire to be admired, applauded, or proven superior.
If you have spent years attacking other Christians without love, repent.
If you have dismissed biblical truth merely to avoid uncomfortable conversations, repent.
If you have treated your church as a substitute for a living relationship with Christ, repent.
If you have walked away from Jesus because people wounded you, consider again the Savior who never promised that His followers would be sinless, but who gave His own life to reconcile sinners to God.
And if you are carrying wounds caused by religious people, healing does not require you to deny what happened.
Bring the truth of those wounds into the light.
Seek trustworthy support.
Remember that forgiveness and reconciliation are not identical, and rebuilding trust requires genuine repentance and accountability.
Christ does not call His sheep to celebrate the behavior of wolves.
He calls them to know His voice.
And His voice still speaks.
“My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me.” — John 10:27, KJV
That is where the question becomes personal again.
Not simply, “Which church is right?”
But, “Am I listening to Jesus?”
Am I following Him when He calls me to forgive?
Am I following Him when He calls me to examine my beliefs?
Am I following Him when He calls me to love the difficult person sitting across the aisle?
Am I following Him when He calls me to stand for truth even when it costs me?
Am I following Him when He calls me to repent of the pride I have disguised as spiritual maturity?
Because the Lord who builds His Church is also the Lord who transforms His people.
And perhaps that is what some of us have been missing.
We have spent so much time asking whether our church has the correct name that we have forgotten to ask whether our lives are bearing His name faithfully.
We have argued over the boundaries of the body while neglecting the commands of its Head.
We have searched for the perfect religious community while resisting the personal holiness to which Jesus calls us.
And still, He has not abandoned His promise.
“I will build my church.”
Not “I might.”
Not “I will try.”
“I will.”
The gates of Hades will not overcome what belongs to Him.
Human pride will not ultimately defeat His purposes.
Historical controversy will not erase His resurrection.
The failures of His followers will not dethrone the King.
But His promise is not permission for complacency.
It is a summons to faithfulness.
And the question of one visible Church versus many denominations must ultimately drive us toward deeper biblical study, not shallow slogans.
The New Testament clearly teaches one body, one Lord, and a unity meant to be expressed in the real life of believers.
It does not provide a simple modern denominational directory.
Christians disagree about which present-day communion most faithfully preserves the visible structure and fullness of the apostolic Church.
Those disagreements deserve serious examination rather than dismissal.
Yet no Christian has permission to make division a virtue, pride a sacrament, or hostility a substitute for holiness.
The Church is called to bear witness to Jesus Christ.
And our responsibility is not merely to defend our understanding of that Church.
It is to obey the Lord who purchased her.
Maybe today you need to stop fighting a brother or sister over an issue you have never seriously studied.
Maybe you need to stop avoiding a difficult truth because it challenges your upbringing.
Maybe you need to apologize to someone you humiliated in the name of defending doctrine.
Maybe you need to return to faithful Christian fellowship after years of isolation.
Maybe you need to ask your pastor a question you have been afraid to ask.
Or maybe, for the first time, you need to surrender your life to Jesus Christ instead of merely inheriting a religious identity.
Whatever the case, do not waste this moment.
Because eternity is too serious for spiritual arrogance.
The Gospel is too precious to be reduced to tribal competition.
And the people Christ calls us to love are too valuable to be treated as disposable.
If this article has challenged something you have believed for years, I would genuinely like to hear from you.
You do not need to pretend you have resolved every theological question.
And you do not need to disclose private wounds to strangers.
You can simply tell us what Scripture has challenged you to reconsider.
If you disagree with this article, you are welcome to explain why with biblical reasoning and respect. Serious discussion is more valuable than empty agreement.
And if you have witnessed genuine Christian love across denominational lines without compromising your convictions, share that testimony.
Someone reading your words may desperately need to know that humility and faithfulness can still exist together.
Not to win an argument.
Not to embarrass another denomination.
But to invite people to examine what Jesus actually said.
Invite your family, friends, struggling believers, seekers, and even those who have become skeptical of Christianity to follow along.
There are people who need more than another religious argument.
They need to encounter the truth and mercy of Jesus Christ.
Gospel Warrior exists to help people encounter Scripture, grow in discipleship, wrestle honestly with difficult questions, and discover the transforming grace of Jesus Christ.
Our desire is to continue this work and expand its reach.
To help more struggling believers.
To encourage people returning to faith.
To reach families searching for biblical guidance.
To make meaningful Christian resources accessible to those who may not otherwise be able to afford them.
Scripture teaches:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” — 2 Corinthians 9:7, KJV
That matters.
Your giving should never be driven by fear, guilt, or the idea that you must pay to glorify God.
You can glorify God through prayer, obedience, generosity, service, sharing biblical truth, and loving your neighbor.
Every sustainable ministry needs people willing to serve, pray, share, create, encourage, and, when possible, give.
These products are not the reason we preach Christ.
They are simply another way to provide useful resources and express appreciation to those helping sustain the ministry.
One thoughtful conversation can open a door.
One Scripture can confront a hardened heart.
One testimony can encourage someone who was ready to give up.
And one person turning to Jesus Christ matters more than any social media metric ever could.
That is the heart behind Gospel Warrior.
Not building a kingdom around a personality.
Not creating another tribe that despises everyone outside it.
But continually pointing people toward the King who gave Himself for sinners.
Jesus Christ.
The crucified Savior.
The risen Lord.
The Head of His Church.
The One who calls His people to repentance, truth, forgiveness, holiness, and love.
And when the noise of religious controversy finally fades, one truth will remain.
The Church was never meant to be a monument to our superiority.
It was meant to bear witness to His glory.
So study deeply.
Ask courageously.
Love faithfully.
Repent sincerely.
And never forget whose Church it is.
Because one day, the arguments that consumed so much of our attention will be measured against the holiness of the Lord we claimed to defend.
And on that day, the question will not be whether we were impressive enough to win every debate.
The question of whether we truly belonged to Christ will matter infinitely more.
The hands that built the Church are the same hands that were pierced to save the people we are so quick to divide.
